questions.q: How does the disk cache differ from .cache() / .persist()?
options: The disk cache is automatic and keyed by file on local SSD; .cache() is explicit and keyed by a specific DataFrame's result in cluster memory
They are two names for the exact same mechanism
The disk cache only works on job clusters, never on all-purpose clusters
.cache() automatically invalidates itself whenever source data changes
questions.explain: The disk cache transparently caches remote file bytes by file; .cache() explicitly materializes one DataFrame's computed result in memory.

questions.q: When does the disk cache help?
options: When the same underlying files are scanned repeatedly by different queries on a long-running cluster
Only on a cluster that terminates immediately after one query
Only when Python UDFs are involved
It never helps — it's purely a compliance feature
questions.explain: A long-running cluster serving many dashboards against the same gold tables benefits repeatedly from the same cached file bytes.

questions.q: Why would caching a DataFrame with .cache() on a job cluster that terminates right after the job provide zero benefit?
options: The cache never outlives the job, so nothing else on that cluster gets the chance to reuse it
Job clusters are physically incapable of running .cache()
.cache() only works on SQL warehouses, not job clusters
Job clusters automatically disable all caching mechanisms
questions.explain: If the cluster terminates immediately afterward, there's no second read to benefit from the cached result — the memory cost bought nothing.

questions.q: What happens to a cached DataFrame if the underlying source data changes after .cache() runs?
options: The cached DataFrame keeps serving the frozen snapshot from when it was cached — it does not automatically refresh
The cache automatically detects the change and recomputes itself
The query immediately fails with an error
The cluster automatically restarts to pick up the new data
questions.explain: .cache() materializes a specific computed result at a point in time; it has no built-in mechanism to notice source data has since changed.

questions.q: What is the key question to ask before deciding to .cache() a DataFrame?
options: Will this exact result get read again on this same cluster before something invalidates it?
Is the DataFrame stored in Delta format?
Does the cluster have Photon enabled?
Is the query running on a SQL warehouse or a notebook?
questions.explain: If the honest answer is 'probably not going to be reused,' caching it is memory pressure with no payoff.
